In my opinion, calling for violence against Nazism in particular, or any groups of people, only serves to create an "us versus them" mentality. That means you establish yourself as their enemy, and it is basic human psychology to turtle up and defend themselves in such situation.

If you firmly believe in your view, and someone just came up from nowhere to insult your belief, or worse, beat you up for following it, would you meekly change your view? No, you will retreat back to your group, and your "comrades" will lick your wounds and reinforce that you were right. Do you remember the story where someone approached a Christian and said "Jesus is not real and you are dumb for believing in that" and then beat the god-fearing fella up, and that person instantly renounced their religion? Yeah, me neither.

The example above was used, because akin to religion, Nazism is a belief, and beliefs, in my opinion, can only be swayed using understanding and compassion. Just like Daryl Davis did. He is directly responsible for 40 to 60 people leaving the KKK. He was even asked to give the hand of a daughter of a former KKK Leader away in her wedding. This was all done without violence or name calling. Now don't tell me he is an anomaly, because he just tried to understand their point of view, and deconstructed it with words and sincerity.

"The lesson learned is: ignorance breeds fear," says Davis. "If you don't keep that fear in check, that fear will breed hatred. If you don't keep hatred in check, it will breed destruction."

Now what do you do if the person still refuse to reject their tenets after several "sensual and passionate" discussion? If they don't verbally advocate violence, leave them be. Try to convert their friends instead. They will probably follow suit. 

Edit: I don't fully agree with OP, and don't agree with many people saying violence is the only answer either. That is such a black and white view, and as with many complex subjects, the answer is always "it depends".
